title: The response to Nepal’s disaster is a test for global climate institutions - Climate Home News
description: The response to Nepal’s disaster is a test for global climate institutions  Climate Home News
publisher.title: Climate Home News
full_article:
Dharam R Uprety is head of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The climate crisis didn’t just knock at our doorstep. It has smashed through homes, demolished critical roads, and caused untold grief for millions of Nepali people. It has now been nearly a month since a wall of ice, rock, and water tore through the Bhote Koshi river system. The death toll has risen to nearly 1,500 people with 5,800 more still missing.

Nepal needs sustained assistance from the international community.

We are staring at a reconstruction bill of at least $5 billion, as we laid out in our letter to the co-chairs of the Board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage on September 1. This constitutes a tenth of our entire economy, and we cannot afford to be saddled with greater loans. We asked the Board to treat the Bhote Koshi disaster as the special case that it is: sudden, unprecedented and exceptional.

The Loss and Damage fund currently holds $820 million in pledges, yet not a single dollar has yet been disbursed for the nearly $3 billion in requests. Its next scheduled meeting is not until December, in Manila. Nepal cannot wait that long, and neither can the next country this happens to.

As loss and damage fund stalls, Nepal crowdfunds flood relief

The tragedy must also serve as a wake up call for immediate climate action. A new study from the World Weather Attribution has found that global warming was a likely contributing factor for the avalanche.

Bandaid solutions are no longer enough; the world needs to transition away from fossil fuels and accelerate investment in clean sources of energy.

Disproportionate impact

The Nepal government has set an ambitious target to replace petrol/diesel vehicles with electric vehicles (EVs) by 2031. The country also already gets most of its electricity from clean sources, with plans for further expansion within the next decade. Our forest cover has grown to 46 percent.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of the planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions. Major polluters need to step up their efforts, so that countries like mine stop bearing a disproportionate impact.

Global emissions are still rising, while countries such as the US, the UK, Australia and several others have drastically reduced the foreign aid that they provide to the rest of the world. And at the same time, they are continuing to increase their fossil fuel production. That is not only unjust, it is also unsustainable for a planet that is already showing us how little room for error remains.

What happened in Bhote Koshi is not unique to the Hindu Kush Himalaya. In May 2025, a nearly identical disaster buried the Swiss village of Blatten, when a rock and ice avalanche tore off the Birch Glacier above it. A study published this month found the avalanche needed almost no friction to travel as far and as fast as it did, a sign of just how destabilised that mountainside had become.

In the Arctic, researchers reported this week that thawing permafrost on the Norwegian island of Jan Mayen turned an ordinary magnitude 6.5 earthquake into the island’s first major glacier rock avalanche in 40 years, the kind of tremor that would once have caused only minor disruption.

From the Alps to the Arctic to the Himalaya, the same warming is loosening the ice and rock that used to hold these mountains together. The next Bhote Koshi could strike anywhere that grip is failing.

Growing focus on mountains in UN climate process

This is not the first time we have tried to get the world’s attention on the mountain ecosystem. At COP30 in Belem last November, Nepal led the push to put mountains on the global climate agenda for the first time, through our Sagarmatha to Belém initiative.

That effort got mountain ecosystems written into the COP30 cover decision and the Global Goal on Adaptation, marking the strongest visibility mountain issues have ever received at the UN climate process. We also secured the first Annual Dialogue on Mountains and Climate Change, which was held at the UN climate talks in June this year at Bonn.

We used COP30 as a platform to warn that retreating glaciers and destabilised mountain systems were not a distant risk. Ten months later, that warning became the Bhote Koshi disaster.

The UN General Assembly and upcoming UN climate talks in Antalya will be two fora for world leaders to show solidarity and more importantly, show how they intend to walk the talk.

Nepal flood destruction shows “limits to adaptation”, scientists say

In the near-term, the Loss and Damage board has been requested to hold an emergency meeting to consider Nepal’s difficult situation. Several nations have generously stepped up to offer physical relief and direct aid. This is greatly welcome. Our needs, unfortunately, far exceed that.

Every impacted village needs a chance to rebuild, children need to see their schools back in operation, and the roads that are the lifeline of communities require urgent reconstruction. Some things may have been lost permanently, but through investment in monitoring and early warning systems, the government of Nepal can try to ensure a future event does not unfold yet another unimaginable tragedy.

This was not just someone else’s disaster that affected the people of Dhading, Rasuwa, and Nuwakot. It is a shared emergency, across Nepal and the world over as more and more communities become victims to a crisis they did not create. This is why, even as we cope with relief and rescue efforts, we are taking the time to present data and share our needs around this climate injustice.

title: How Nepal can lead the global climate charge at UNGA 81 and beyond - The Kathmandu Post
description: How Nepal can lead the global climate charge at UNGA 81 and beyond  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s maiden address to the United Nations General Assembly on September 24, 2026, is expected to focus on climate change and climate justice, in light of Nepal’s recent catastrophic ‘Himalayan Tsunami’.

Steered by Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, Nepal will also host a high-level side event on ‘Sagarmatha to the Sea: A Call to Action for a Climate-Resilient Future’. Nepal is expected to highlight this same issue at several ministerial meetings of the Least Developed Countries (LDCs), Landlocked Developing Countries (LLDCs), the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), and the Group of 77 and China.

All of this will launch Nepal’s call for climate justice and international assistance for climate-vulnerable countries that contribute little to greenhouse gas emissions and global warming but suffer disproportionately from their impacts. High mountain regions, small islands and coastal states are particularly vulnerable to such impacts.

The UNGA 81 offers a good, high-level forum to launch Nepal’s appeal. However, given the many other competing priorities, ranging from issues of war and peace, trade and commerce, and artificial intelligence to other pressing global concerns, the issue of climate justice is unlikely to be dealt with decisively at the UNGA alone. Along with other climate-vulnerable countries and like-minded stakeholders, Nepal should persevere in taking this issue to other relevant forums where climate justice will be central rather than peripheral.

One such forum will be COP31, the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC (UN Framework Convention on Climate Change), which will be held in Antalya, Türkiye, on November 9-20. COP31 is a major international summit to negotiate global climate action, review progress under the 2015 Paris Agreement, and address issues of long-term climate financing, such as the Loss and Damage Fund to respond to the impacts of climate-induced disasters, the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility, and issues related to science and technology to alleviate the impacts of climate change.

It is important for Nepal to prepare itself well to participate effectively, and even take a leadership role, at COP31 and in its follow-up. Three urgent and important tasks for Nepal are constituting a strong official representation, forging a strong partnership with other countries, and developing close contacts with the COP31 presidency.

A strong official team to represent Nepal at COP31 should designate highly qualified Nepali experts to attend and influence negotiations in various sub-committees of the conference. There is also room for independent civil society activists to attend and influence COP31. The government should encourage and collaborate with Nepali NGOs, academics and activists who plan to attend COP31.

To forge a strong partnership with other climate-vulnerable countries, Nepal needs to look to those from the Hindu Kush Himalaya region, small island states in the Caribbean, Pacific, and Indian Ocean regions, and Nepal’s natural partners among the least-developed and landlocked states and neighbouring coastal states.

Nepal also needs to develop close contacts with the COP31 Presidency of Türkiye and its close partner Australia. If Nepal’s advocacy is framed as ‘Sagarmatha to the Sea’, Australia is likely to be a strong supporter of Nepal, given the long history of cooperation between Nepal and Australia. Australia and New Zealand are very close to and supportive of the climate-vulnerable Pacific Island states. Hence, this framing is likely to attract strong support from Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific Islands.

Besides these three big priorities, Nepal should also forge strategic partnerships with a number of other influential stakeholders. These would include Chris Bowen, Minister for Climate Change and Energy of Australia, who has been assigned as President of Negotiations for the duration of COP31; his colleague Julia Gardiner, who chairs the Subsidiary Body for Implementation of UNFCCC commitments ; the UNFCCC Secretariat in Bonn, Germany, which prepares most of the documents submitted for consideration at various COPs; the government of Ethiopia, which will host COP32 in 2027; and prominent climate activists like Greta Thunberg and others who have spoken strongly in solidarity with Nepal.

Nepal should mobilise all its embassies in relevant countries to explain and advocate its position with relevant authorities and individuals. As Nepal does not have diplomatic missions in many small island states, the Nepal missions to the UN in New York and Geneva should be tasked with fostering partnerships with those countries.

COP31 has an extensive agenda and many committees and working groups. It will not be possible for Nepal’s relatively small official delegation to attend and influence all of them. Hence, it should pick and choose a handful of committees and working groups where it will focus its attention, while encouraging other like-minded countries and Nepali civil society activists to cover those agenda items and committees that are also important but of secondary interest to Nepal.

Besides the important plenaries and ministerial roundtables, which Nepal should definitely attend at the highest level possible, Nepal should strive to attend and influence at COP31 by participating in matters relating to long-term climate finance, the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, capacity-building and technology transfer to the least developed countries, and matters relating to gender and climate change.

In each of these areas, it is important for designated members of the Nepali delegation to do their homework, read the background reports prepared by the UNFCCC Secretariat, try to understand the negotiating positions of various groups of delegates, and formulate Nepal’s preferred position well in advance of COP31. In some of these areas, Nepal should strive to take a leadership position while being supportive of other like-minded delegates.

The special vulnerability of the high mountains, with the fragility of a large number of glacial lakes, compounded by the melting of permafrost on their mountain slopes, as in the case of the Nepal Himalayas, is not a separate and specific item on the agenda of COP31. Nepal should seek every opportunity to get this issue included in debates under all relevant agenda items.

COP27 had requested the Secretariat of the Climate Fund to include a summary of key findings on progress towards achieving the goal of mobilising $100 billion per year to address the needs of developing countries in the context of meaningful mitigation actions and transparency on implementation, for consideration at COP31.

The world is nowhere near the goal of mobilising that amount per annum. The current international atmosphere is not conducive to mobilising such an amount, given the recent trend in many rich and powerful countries to reduce overseas development assistance (ODA), increase military spending, even denying the existence of climate change, and prioritise other national and parochial concerns.

In this context, while not compromising on already agreed global commitments, Nepal and like-minded countries might consider coming up with more modest but pragmatic short-term proposals that address the acute and proven needs of the most vulnerable countries. Nepal’s own need for massive post-disaster reconstruction in the affected areas is generally appreciated by most countries and organisations. So is the need for a more robust early warning system to be developed in close partnership with our immediate neighbours, China and India, preferably coordinated by ICIMOD.

title: One month after the floods, efforts to restore education are helping children return to learning in Nepal - Unicef
description: One month after the floods, efforts to restore education are helping children return to learning in Nepal  Unicef
publisher.title: Unicef
full_article:
KATHMANDU, 23 September 2026 – One month after devastating floods struck central and northern Nepal, thousands of children continue to face disruptions to their education, highlighting the urgent need for sustained support to help them return to safe learning environments.

Initial assessments indicate that learning has been disrupted for more than 14,000 children across 62 schools and learning centres in flood-affected areas in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts. The disaster also had a devastating human toll, with around 440 students and education personnel reported dead or missing, including 414 children.

"Education is a critical part of children's recovery after a disaster," said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative to Nepal. "Returning to learning provides children with a sense of stability, routine and hope at a time when many have experienced significant loss and uncertainty."

Since the onset of the emergency, UNICEF has worked with the Government of Nepal and partners to help children resume learning as quickly as possible. To date, UNICEF has supported the establishment of 48 temporary learning centres, helping more than 1,400 children in flood-affected areas return to learning. UNICEF has also provided essential learning materials and psychosocial support to help children recover and continue their education.

While these efforts are helping children return to learning, recovery needs remain substantial. The Education Rapid Needs Assessment estimates that significant investment will be required to restore damaged education infrastructure and ensure children can continue their education uninterrupted.

UNICEF is calling for continued support for both immediate recovery efforts and longer-term resilience building, ensuring that every child affected by the floods can learn, recover and thrive. As Nepal moves from emergency response to recovery, there is also an opportunity to strengthen the resilience of schools, health facilities, water and sanitation systems, and other critical infrastructure to better withstand future shocks. With climate-related disasters becoming more frequent and severe, investments in climate-resilient infrastructure, preparedness and social services are critical to help protect children and communities from future disruptions.

"When floods damage schools, children don't just lose classrooms. We miss lessons, fall behind in our studies, spend less time with our friends and teachers, and lose the routines that help us feel safe and supported," said Jayanti Bam, UNICEF Nepal's Youth Advocate for Climate Action. "We need stronger schools that can withstand disasters. We also need to know what to do when there is a flood, landslide, or other emergency. And if our schools are damaged, we need ways to keep learning, whether in a temporary learning space or online, so our education can continue."

One month after the floods, thousands of children and their families are still enduring the consequences every day. Many families remaindisplaced, some schools are still being used as temporary shelters, and damaged roads and bridges continue to limit access to critical education, health, water and sanitation services in some of the hardest-hit communities.

title: Self-compunction must to retain institutional dignity of journalism: Info Minister Dr Timilsina - The Rising Nepal
description: Self-compunction must to retain institutional dignity of journalism: Info Minister Dr Timilsina  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Sept 23: Minister for Information and Communications, Dr Bikram Timilsina, has said the journalism sector ought to seriously review its weaknesses, make corrections and advance by maintaining professionalism, credibility and institutional dignity.

Addressing a programme organized to hand over the 'Hem-Sunil Television Journalism Award for Courageous Reporting-2083' in the federal capital on Wednesday, Minister Dr Timilsina viewed journalism is an institution in itself, so it requires responsibility to uphold prestige, dignity, and credibility with collective efforts of individual journalist, institution and entire journalism fraternity.

The programme was organized by the Federation of Nepali Journalists (FNJ) chapter at Nepal Television.

"Every journalist must reflect on the elements that undermine the prestige of journalism," the Minister stressed. He argued answers must be sought to the key concerns regarding the kind of journalism and media institutions we want to create and foster.

According to him, serious questions were being raised on the safety and professionalism of journalism and future of journalists. Considering this, government has been forwarding necessary initiatives to address the concerns. "The tendency to take to the streets and blame each other over minor issues would not help wipe out systemic problems. Rather strengthening established procedures, statutes and institutional systems help address the problems in this sector," the Minister reminded.

The Minister pointed to the urgency of reviewing the status of public media institutions, including the agencies of public service broadcasting. He, however, reminded the public media's long history and contributions to the development of Nepali music, media and journalism. It is essential to study the reasons behind the deterioration of public media, according to him.





"Why the media institutions despite owning the property worth billions of rupees seek help from State to manage employees' pensions and benefits? What are the factors hindering the audits for years? We must find answers to these pressing questions," Minister Timilsina became vocal, seeking transparency at public media. The physical infrastructures of the Radio Nepal and the Nepal Television are not subpar to private organizations, but why these institutions were yet to become robust, he wondered further.

The Minister urged these media to seek answers within the organizations themselves.

In his argument, institutional reform is prerequisite for bolstering public media agencies and the journalism sector in a whole. He underscored all sides' preparation to rectify weaknesses and malpractices.

The Minister observed that as journalism is a profession that faces risks, the journalists must prioritize their individual safety. Those undertaking reporting assignments at risky circumstances can inform the public to avoid adversity. Individual safety must be prioritized while fulfilling professional duties whenever possible.

Five journalists were honoured on the occasion with the 'Hem-Sunil Television Journalism Award for Courageous Reporting-2083'.Those receiving the award are Ramchandra Aryal (correspondent) and Diwakar Pokharel (cameraperson) of Himalaya Television and Shyam Shrestha (cameraperson) of Kantipur Television.

Even Shiva Silwal (Dhading correspondent) and Anjir Singh BK (Bhaktapur correspondent) of Nepal Television were honoured for their news coverage on climate change and environmental risks.

The Nepal Television chapter of FNJ has been conferring the award every year in memory of Hem Bhandari and Sunil Singh since 2064 BS. Bhandari and Singh, the reporters with the Nepal Television, died in a helicopter crash in 2063BS at Ghunsha, Taplejung district.

Environmentalists and dignitaries, including Minister of State for Forest and Soil Conservation, Gopal Rai, had died in the tragic incident. (RSS)

Mita and Hemant Parikh from Georgia, USA, survived a catastrophic flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border after taking a spontaneous detour to view Mount Everest.

The couple were on a long-planned pilgrimage to Mount Kailash with a 47-strong international group, none of whom have been found alongside their seven guides.

The August flash flood, likely triggered by a collapsed glacier, left over 1,400 people dead and 5,000 missing, including at least 80 US citizens.

Nepal's finance minister warned the ultimate death toll could approach that of the 2015 earthquake, which claimed over 9,000 lives.

Reconstruction costs across Nepal are estimated at nearly $5 billion, with disaster aid funding set to be discussed at the UN General Assembly.

Kathmandu, Sept 23: Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has expressed commitment to continuing Nepal's contribution to United Nations peacekeeping missions aimed at promoting global peace and security.

During a sideline meeting in New York with UN Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations, Jean-Pierre Lacroix, Minister Khanal, who is attending the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, expressed gratitude for the trust the United Nations has consistently shown toward Nepali peacekeepers.

He also said Nepal attaches great importance to its long-standing partnership with the United Nations and wishes to further strengthen this relationship built on mutual trust, respect, and cooperation in the days ahead. "Nepal stands ready to contribute up to 10,000 peacekeepers should the need arise and a request be made by the United Nations."

"Nepal has consistently cooperated by extending the tenure of officers, deploying peacekeeping contingents via commercial flights, making necessary adjustments to logistics and equipment transport arrangements, and implementing other cost-reduction measures as requested by the United Nations," he said and urged that Nepal's sustained contributions, commitment, and cooperation in the field of peacekeeping be duly recognized in future deployment opportunities.

On the occasion, Under-Secretary-General Jean-Pierre Lacroix commended the role played by Nepal and its security personnel in global peacekeeping missions. (RSS)

full_article:
US Pledges $31 Million for Nepal Flood Relief, Recovery

WASHINGTON, DC- The United States announced plans to provide an additional $31 million to support Nepal’s recovery from devastating floods, including funding for permanent bridges, humanitarian assistance and drones manufactured in the US.

The announcement came as about 70 Americans remained unaccounted for following the disaster.

US Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker announced the proposed assistance during a meeting with Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal in New York, according to the US State Department.

Hooker conveyed US sympathies to those affected by the floods, including families of Americans whose whereabouts remained unknown.

The largest component of the package is $13 million for US-manufactured drones intended to strengthen Nepal’s ability to respond to future disasters and support recovery operations.

The State Department did not provide details about the type or number of drones under consideration or identify the US manufacturers that could supply them.

Washington also plans to work with Congress to provide $10 million for permanent, custom-built bridges. The bridges will be sourced from an American company, the department said.

The proposed bridges are intended to restore transport links damaged by the flooding and improve regional connectivity in affected areas. Roads and bridges are particularly important in Nepal, where difficult mountain terrain can leave communities isolated after floods and landslides.

Another $8 million will be directed towards water, sanitation and hygiene services, as well as shelter, protection and livelihood assistance.

Part of that allocation will support winterization programmes for communities facing colder weather without adequate housing or infrastructure.

The State Department said the new announcement would raise total US assistance for Nepal’s flood response and recovery to more than $36 million.

“The United States will continue to work closely with the Government of Nepal to identify and deliver additional assistance where it is most needed,” the department said.

September 22 meeting took place on the sidelines of high-level diplomatic engagements in New York, where world leaders and senior officials had gathered for the United Nations General Assembly.

US authorities are also working to locate American citizens caught in the affected areas. Earlier reports said some Americans had reached safety, but the new State Department statement said approximately 70 remained unaccounted for. (IANS)

title: Climate disasters are growing. So are cuts to programs that prepare for them - Boston Herald
description: Climate disasters are growing. So are cuts to programs that prepare for them  Boston Herald
publisher.title: Boston Herald
full_article:
By VICTORIA MILKO and SIBI ARASU

KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Sitting on the floor of a makeshift shelter for survivors of Nepal’s deadly recent floods, Tenzin Dolma Ghale said she had nothing left but the clothes she was wearing. Her entire village and members of her family were washed away by the surge of water and debris that killed over 1,450 people and left more than 6,000 missing.

After speaking, she waved a hand and looked at the ground. “It’s all finished,” she said.

Ghale is among millions of people living with the deadly consequences of climate-related disasters. As such disasters intensify, international climate adaptation and disaster preparedness aid programs have been slashed, leaving countries facing billions of dollars in avoidable damage and dwindling recovery funds.

“The reality is that we need trillions of dollars every year, but developed countries have not met their obligation,” said Harjeet Singh, founding director of New Delhi-based Satat Sampada Climate Foundation.

Aid cuts weaken disaster monitoring in the Himalayas

The Trump administration’s abrupt cuts to U.S. foreign aid in 2025 eliminated or sharply curtailed programs serving millions of people worldwide, with devastating consequences for many communities. Reductions by other major donor countries deepened the funding crisis.

Among the programs shut was SERVIR-Hindu Kush Himalaya, a joint initiative of the U.S. Agency for International Development, NASA and the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD.

Covering Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan, the program used satellites and geospatial analysis for disaster risk reduction, water resources and land cover. It facilitated flood risk services, collaboration with the Nepal Red Cross Society on risk communication and more than 170 public data sets on glaciers, disasters and vulnerability.

Glacial and disaster preparedness experts praised the organization for its extensive research, cross-border coordination and support of local disaster reduction measures.

Before losing its funding due to USAID cuts, the program addressed mounting risks in a region where climate change has caused rapid glacier melt, shifting monsoons and increasingly frequent floods, landslides and glacial lake outburst floods, or GLOFs. Those changes endangered food, water and energy security for nearly 2 billion people living in or downstream of the region, according to ICIMOD.

Himalayan glaciers are losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, according to a new report by global consultancy Systemiq, produced with ICIMOD. Yet only around 0.1% of the Himalaya’s estimated 40,000 glaciers are currently monitored in detail and on a sustained basis, the report said.

When funding for SERVIR-HKH ended, so did programs that monitored landslide forecasting, daily flooding, training programs and regional collaboration between countries.

With the program’s loss, millions now face a heightened risk of GLOFs, which can release millions of cubic meters of water and debris in just a few hours.

In northern Pakistan, melting glaciers have created 3,044 glacial lakes, with over 30 identified as likely to result in such floods in areas where over 7 million people live, according to the United Nations Development Program.

Afghanistan also faces an increased threat of GLOFs, according to research published by the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.

In India — which was not part of the SERVIR-HKH program but borders all of the countries that were and is also home to over half the Himalayas — over 130 high-altitude lakes are at risk of flooding.

South Asia is already experiencing deadly climate-related disasters. The 2022 Pakistan floods killed more than 1,700 people and caused an estimated $40 billion in damage. Flooding in Nepal in 2025 killed nine people and caused millions of dollars in damage. Cloudbursts, landslides, flash floods and extreme rainfall have wreaked havoc in the Indian Himalayas, resulting in the death of over 12,000 people and damage exceeding billions of dollars in the last 15 years.

The region suffered economic losses of at least $7 billion in 2025 due to climate-driven extreme weather, according to the Emergency Events Database maintained by the University of Louvain, Belgium. This database itself is at risk of being shut down as a result of USAID funding cuts.

In a statement to The Associated Press, the U.S. State Department said that the U.S. supports Nepal’s flood warning capacity through programs with the World Meteorological Organization and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The department noted that SERVIR-HKH ended in January 2025 but that its tools remain active through ICIMOD.

The impact extends beyond communities hit directly. The Himalayan region is vital to national economies, with agriculture, industry, tourism and domestic use all dependent upon it.

Cuts to programs like SERVIR-HKH will have cascading effects for years, said Neha Rai, a climate finance expert at ICIMOD.

Rai likened the cuts to climate programs to abruptly halting funds for cancer research, which needs years of sustained research for success.

“Climate risk is also a generational challenge,” said Rai. “You need long-term observations, expertise, you need institutions that cannot simply be switched off and on as short-term priorities.”

Rai said cuts to cross-border programs have also impacted information sharing between governments, scientists and organizations across the region — a critical function in a region where what happens upstream directly affects countries downstream.

Climate finance shrinks as vulnerable countries face rising debt

These cuts are part of a larger trend. According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, official development assistance from its Development Assistance Committee members, which includes the U.S., fell 23% in 2025 — the largest annual contraction on record. Traditionally large donors such as the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Japan and Canada have also announced massive reductions, reallocating funds to defense and other domestic priorities.

Global South countries spend approximately 225 times more in debt repayments than what they receive in grant-based climate finance, according to a recent report by the advocacy group, ActionAid International.

“There is a toxic relationship, in fact, between the climate crisis and the debt crisis,” said Teresa Andersen of ActionAid International.

She said countries take loans to recover from climate impacts but then cut investments in clean energy and preparations for future climate-related extreme weather to repay the loans.

The money being provided isn’t nearly enough, and climate often isn’t prioritized, said Richard Sherman, a board member of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, an international climate finance mechanism to assist developing countries vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change.

“There’s plenty of money if it goes to certain priorities, but for climate change right now, we’re witnessing a severe depreciation of the importance to act and make systems more resilient,” he said.

While disaster recovery funds still exist, they’re also losing funding and aren’t equipped to handle the expected increase in disasters, he said.

“We’re not expecting developed countries to act as an ATM,” said Sherman. “But supporting vulnerable countries, helping them adapt and become more resilient means they’re less likely to suffer the kind of impacts we have right now.”

Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India.

The Sherpa and Nepali community of Sonoma Valley raised $100,275 during a Tuesday, Sept. 22, fundraiser to support relief and rescue efforts after floods in central Nepal killed more than 1,000 people and left thousands of others missing.

The event was hosted by The Himalayan Sherpa Club of Sonoma, a local nonprofit and close to 50 of its volunteers.

Pemba Sherpa, a member of the organization, said close to 500 people attended the event.

“A lot of people showed up there to support us and their eyes have filled up with tears,” Sherpa said. “People left very happy and they did whatever they could.”

title: Georgia couple who survived Nepal floods recall life-saving chance decision - New York Post
description: Georgia couple who survived Nepal floods recall life-saving chance decision  New York Post
publisher.title: New York Post
full_article:
A Georgia couple who narrowly escaped Nepal’s deadly August flooding recalled the precise moment that a last-minute decision took them out of the path of devastation.

Mita and Hemant Parikh, of Suwanee, were in the area after planning for 15 years to make a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in the Himalayas in Tibet, a sacred site in Hinduism.

“Everybody has a bucket list, but this bucket list, you don’t choose it,” Mita told CBS Atlanta. “God chooses for you.”

5 Mita and Hemant Parikh reflect on surviving a deadly flood in Nepal. CBS Atlanta/Youtube

They were joined by 47 travelers including families from Australia, other parts of the US and elsewhere, with seven guides leading the group.

On impulse, the couple decided to take a side trip to view Mount Everest, the world’s tallest peak, which turned out to be a life-saving excursion.

“Usually we argue, or tickets are expensive — no, let’s not go,” Mita recalled to the outlet. “But I don’t know why we both agreed.”

After veering off the planned travel route to catch a glimpse of the legendary mountain, they were going to return to the group with another guide who helped them reach the Everest viewing point, only to find their hotel had been washed away by the floods.

5 An aerial view shows destroyed houses and roads covered in mud along the Trishuli River, following a landslide and flash floods in areas near the Nepal-China border. The death toll from the disaster has risen to more than 530, with hundreds of people missing. Anadolu via Getty Images

5 An aerial view shows the aftermath of flooding along the Bhotekoshi River, which affected low-lying areas and settlements near the riverbanks in Nuwakot, Nepal. The flooding caused widespread damage to homes, roads, a bridge, and a hydropower station, with search and rescue operations underway for several missing people. NurPhoto via Getty Images

Several families from the group, and all of the guides, are among the more than 6,000 people reported missing — including 85 Americans, according to AP.

“As soon as I close my eyes, I see Kailash, and I see the people,” Mita told CBS Atlanta. “I don’t know what happened.”

5 The aftermath of devastating flash floods is seen in Nuwakot, Bagmati province, as people in the affected areas return to the ruins of their homes to search for belongings. Anadolu via Getty Images

5 Nepali hydropower worker Sanjay Sah, left, breaks down after meeting his mother at his residence in Nepal’s Saptari district, after being rescued from a flooded tunnel in the aftermath of deadly flash floods. Sah survived for 10 days in darkness inside the flooded tunnel, drinking muddy water and losing all sense of time as he prayed for rescue. AFP via Getty Images

“I ask myself why?” Hemant said, dumbfounded that he and his wife might be the only two from the group to make it out alive. “And I don’t have an answer.”
